slides.title: Normalization: The Discipline of Dependency Hygiene
slides.subtitle: Eliminating redundancy and preserving truth in relational databases
agenda: Why atomicity is the foundation of truth (1NF)
Trade-offs: lossless joins, dependency preservation, and performance
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome. Today we explore normalization—not as a dry database rulebook, but as a rigorous method for encoding truth. We'll see how poor dependency design leads to silent data contradictions, and how 1NF through BCNF progressively eliminate them. Along the way, we'll uncover parallels in software engineering and security. By the end, you'll be able to diagnose flawed schemas and decompose them correctly.

slides.title: Anomalies Reveal Hidden Dependency Flaws
bullets: Update anomalies occur when one fact is stored in multiple rows, risking inconsistency
Deletion anomalies erase critical data when removing a single tuple
Insertion anomalies prevent adding facts unless unrelated data is present
These symptoms trace back to improper functional dependencies in the schema
Normalization resolves these by isolating dependencies into dedicated relations
slides.speaker_notes: Imagine updating a course textbook in an enrollment table and only changing some rows. The database now contradicts itself—not due to user error, but because the schema allows multiple sources of truth. This update anomaly is a red flag. Similarly, deleting the last student in a course shouldn’t erase the course’s instructor. These are not bugs—they’re design failures rooted in uncontrolled dependencies.

slides.title: 1NF: Atomicity Enables Reliable Data Control
bullets: Each attribute must contain indivisible, atomic values—no lists or nested structures
Duplicate rows are disallowed; a candidate key ensures tuple uniqueness
Non-atomic fields like 'Math, Physics' prevent indexing and constraint enforcement
Atomicity allows precise functional dependencies and prevents parsing vulnerabilities
Even JSON or arrays in RDBMS bypass traditional normalization safeguards
slides.speaker_notes: First Normal Form is not optional—it’s the bedrock. Without atomic values, you cannot define clean functional dependencies. Consider a field storing comma-separated courses: you can’t enforce referential integrity, index efficiently, or query reliably. Worse, in security contexts, such fields enable injection attacks. Atomicity isn’t neatness—it’s a prerequisite for truth and safety.

slides.title: 1NF Formal Definition
slides.equation_tex: \text{A relation is in 1NF iff:}\\\text{1. All attribute values are atomic}\\\text{2. Tuples are unique}\\\text{3. Row/column order is irrelevant}
slides.equation_caption: 1NF enforces structural simplicity: one fact per cell, no duplicates.
bullets: Atomicity ensures each value can be individually constrained and indexed
Uniqueness is enforced via candidate keys, not application logic
Order irrelevance aligns with the relational model’s set semantics
Most RDBMS enforce 1NF by default for scalar types
slides.speaker_notes: This equation captures the three pillars of 1NF. Atomicity ensures that every cell holds a single, indivisible fact. Uniqueness means no two rows are identical—enforced by keys. And order doesn’t matter: relations are sets, not lists. Violate any of these, and higher normal forms collapse. For example, a JSON array in a column may seem convenient, but it breaks atomicity and disables standard FD reasoning.

slides.title: Fix This: Events Table in 1NF
slides.exercise_prompt: You are given a table Events(Location, Dates) where Dates contains values like '2025-04-01, 2025-04-05'. (a) Explain why this violates 1NF. (b) Redesign the schema to achieve 1NF. (c) Define a candidate key and a constraint to prevent duplicates.
bullets: Hint: Identify the non-atomic attribute and split it into rows
Hint: The new key should combine Location and the individual date
Consider how this change enables date-based queries and constraints
slides.speaker_notes: Take three minutes on this. The core issue is that 'Dates' holds multiple values, making it impossible to query or constrain individual dates. The fix is to create one row per date. The new key becomes (Location, Date), ensuring no duplicates. This transformation enables reliable indexing, constraints, and queries—demonstrating how atomicity unlocks control.

slides.title: 2NF: Eliminate Partial Key Dependencies
bullets: A relation must be in 1NF and have no partial dependencies on composite keys
Partial dependency: a non-prime attribute depends on part of a candidate key
Example: Instructor depends only on Course, not (StudentID, Course)
Such dependencies cause redundancy and deletion anomalies
Fix by decomposing—projecting out the dependent attributes into new tables
slides.speaker_notes: Second Normal Form targets a subtle flaw: when a non-prime attribute depends on only part of a composite key. For instance, in Enrollments(StudentID, Course, Instructor), if Course → Instructor, then Instructor depends only on Course—half the key. This forces repetition: every student in Math101 stores Dr. Lee. Worse, deleting the last student deletes Dr. Lee’s association. The fix? Extract Course → Instructor into its own table.

slides.title: 2NF Formal Definition
slides.equation_tex: \text{R is in 2NF iff:}\\\text{1. R is in 1NF}\\\text{2. Every non-prime attribute}\\\text{is fully functionally dependent}\\\text{on every candidate key}
slides.equation_caption: No non-prime attribute should depend on a subset of a key.
bullets: Full functional dependence means the entire key is needed to determine the attribute
Partial dependencies create redundancy and update hazards
Decomposition removes the dependency from the original table
The extracted FD forms a new relation with its determinant as key
slides.speaker_notes: This definition is precise: if any non-prime attribute can be determined by a proper subset of a candidate key, 2NF is violated. For example, in R(A,B,C) with key {A,B} and A → C, then C depends only on A—a partial dependency. The fix is to split into R1(A,C) and R2(A,B), eliminating redundancy. This is not just cleanup—it’s preventing future data lies.

slides.title: Diagnose and Fix: EmployeeSkills Table
slides.exercise_prompt: Given EmployeeSkills(EmpID, Skill, Certification, SkillLevel) with candidate key {EmpID, Skill} and FD: Skill → Certification. (a) Is this in 2NF? (b) If not, identify the partial dependency. (c) Decompose the schema into 2NF.
bullets: Hint: Check if Certification depends on the full key or part of it
Hint: Skill is part of the key, so Skill → Certification is a partial dependency
The decomposition should isolate the Skill → Certification dependency
slides.speaker_notes: This is a classic 2NF trap. Certification depends only on Skill, not on (EmpID, Skill). So every time a skill appears, its certification is repeated. Decompose into SkillCert(Skill, Certification) and EmployeeSkill(EmpID, Skill, SkillLevel). Now, certification is stored once per skill. This eliminates redundancy and prevents update anomalies.

slides.title: 3NF: Break Transitive Dependency Chains
bullets: A relation is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and has no transitive dependencies
Transitive dependency: A → B and B → C implies A → C through B
Example: Course → Instructor and Instructor → Textbook creates indirect dependency
This allows contradictions: changing instructor without updating textbook
Decompose so each FD has a superkey or involves only prime attributes
slides.speaker_notes: Third Normal Form stops ripple effects. If Course determines Instructor, and Instructor determines Textbook, then Textbook is transitively dependent on Course. But if you update the instructor and forget the textbook, you create a contradiction. 3NF eliminates this by requiring that non-prime attributes depend only on superkeys or on prime attributes. The fix? Split Instructor → Textbook into its own table.

slides.title: 3NF Formal Definition
slides.equation_tex: \text{R is in 3NF iff:}\\\text{For every non-trivial } X \rightarrow Y,\\\text{either } X \text{ is a superkey,}\\\text{or } Y \text{ is a prime attribute}
slides.equation_caption: Every dependency must be on a superkey or to a key part.
bullets: This blocks non-prime attributes from depending on non-superkeys
Prime attributes can depend on non-superkeys—this is allowed
Transitive dependencies on non-prime attributes violate 3NF
Decomposition ensures each FD lives in a table where its determinant is a key
slides.speaker_notes: This definition is subtle but powerful. If X → Y and X isn't a superkey, then Y must be prime—part of some candidate key. This exception allows some flexibility. But in the Course → Instructor → Textbook chain, Textbook is non-prime and depends on Instructor, which is not a superkey. So it violates 3NF. The fix? Create InstructorTextbook(Instructor, Textbook), making Instructor the key.

slides.title: BCNF: Only Superkeys May Determine Attributes
bullets: BCNF is stricter: every non-trivial X → Y requires X to be a superkey
It eliminates all functional dependency anomalies, even when 3NF allows them
Example: Course → Time in Teaching(Professor, Course, Time) violates BCNF
Decomposition may lose dependencies or require lossy joins
BCNF guarantees no anomalies but may sacrifice practicality
slides.speaker_notes: Boyce-Codd Normal Form is the gold standard. Unlike 3NF, it doesn’t allow exceptions for prime attributes. If any non-superkey determines anything, it’s a violation. For example, in Teaching(Professor, Course, Time) with Course → Time, Course isn’t a superkey—so it violates BCNF. Decomposing into CourseTime(Course, Time) and ProfCourse(Professor, Course) fixes it, but we lose the original dependency {Professor, Time} → Course. This is the trade-off: purity vs. dependency preservation.

slides.title: BCNF Decomposition: StudentMajorAdvisor
slides.exercise_prompt: Given StudentMajorAdvisor(Student, Major, Advisor) with FDs: Major → Advisor and Student → Major, and key {Student}. (a) Is this in BCNF? (b) If not, identify the violating FD. (c) Decompose into BCNF. (d) Does the decomposition preserve all FDs?
bullets: Hint: Check if Major → Advisor has a superkey on the left
Hint: Major is not a superkey, so it violates BCNF
Decompose into MajorAdvisor(Major, Advisor) and StudentMajor(Student, Major)
slides.speaker_notes: This schema is in 3NF but not BCNF. Why? Because Major → Advisor, but Major is not a superkey. Student → Major is fine—Student is the key. To achieve BCNF, split into MajorAdvisor(Major, Advisor) and StudentMajor(Student, Major). The join is lossless, and all FDs are preserved. This is a rare case where BCNF doesn’t force a trade-off—lucky!

slides.title: Trade-offs: Lossless Joins and Dependency Preservation
bullets: Lossless join decomposition ensures no spurious tuples on reconstruction
Dependency preservation allows enforcing all FDs in the decomposed schema
BCNF guarantees no anomalies but may not preserve dependencies
3NF always allows both lossless join and dependency-preserving decomposition
In practice, 3NF is often preferred for balance
slides.speaker_notes: Normalization isn’t free. BCNF eliminates all anomalies but may force you to check dependencies globally—defeating the purpose of decomposition. 3NF, by allowing prime attribute exceptions, ensures we can always decompose into a form that’s both lossless and dependency-preserving. That’s why many real-world designs stop at 3NF: it offers strong guarantees without impractical overhead.

slides.title: Normalization: Truth Through Dependency Control
bullets: 1NF ensures atomicity—facts are isolatable and enforceable
2NF eliminates partial dependencies on composite keys
3NF stops transitive dependencies for non-prime attributes
BCNF demands that only superkeys determine attributes
Trade-offs exist: BCNF prevents anomalies but may lose dependencies
slides.speaker_notes: Normalization is diagnostic surgery on data dependencies. Start with 1NF: are your facts atomic? Then 2NF: are you storing facts about key parts? Then 3NF: are dependencies chaining through non-keys? Finally, BCNF: are only superkeys determining values? Each step removes a class of lies. But remember: 3NF is often the sweet spot, offering strong guarantees while preserving dependencies. Use this discipline not just in databases—but in any system where truth matters.
